# Semestral project catalogue {.unnumbered}

These topics are starting points for independent study and your own project
formulation. Follow the [project proposal requirements](semestral-project.qmd#sec-semestral-project-proposal).

## Equilibrium computation in stochastic games {#sec-project-stochastic-games}

Stochastic games generalize Markov decision processes (MDPs) to settings with multiple interacting players. Compute stationary Nash equilibrium policies and state values for a discounted two-player zero-sum stochastic game. For the model and value-iteration
algorithm, see [*Pursuit-Evasion Games II*](../presentations/b4m36uir-lec10-slidesTK.pdf).

**Possible application: robotic pursuit-evasion.**

This [task](https://cw.fel.cvut.cz/b221/courses/uir/hw/t4c-vi)
provides inspiration and a starting point: one player controls a single evading robot and
the other jointly controls two pursuers on a grid map with obstacles.
In a fully observed model, the state records all three robot positions.
The pursuers seek capture, while the evader tries to avoid it. The
assignment uses opposite capture rewards and discounting to favour earlier
capture; its resource pack provides maps and a simulation environment.

Compute randomized policies for both players and values for the initial
configurations, using value iteration with linear programming for the matrix
games at each state. Possible questions include how obstacles and starting
positions affect coordinated pursuit, or how computation time grows with map
size. Choose one focused question and a manageable set of maps.

In your proposal, specify movement, capture and termination rules, rewards and
discounting. Explain how any simulation step limit relates to the discounted
model. Plan small, hand-checkable cases and a numerical check of equilibrium
quality, such as each player's possible gain from a best response.

## Double Oracle algorithm for matrix games {#sec-project-double-oracle}

Implement Double Oracle for two-player zero-sum matrix games. Study the
[Double Oracle section of Lecture 4](../lectures/04-two-player-zero-sum-games.qmd#sec-zero-sum-double-oracle)
and, for further information, the [*Double Oracle Algorithm* slides](<../presentations/DO lecture MFF 2025.pdf>).

**Possible application: pursuit-evasion with planned paths.**

You can check the maps, four-neighbour moves and capture rules from this
[task](https://cw.fel.cvut.cz/b221/courses/uir/hw/t4a-greedy).
One possible formulation fixes initial positions, one evader, one or two
pursuers, and a short horizon $H$. A pure strategy is a legal $H$-step path
for the evader, or a joint choice of paths for the pursuing team. Both players
commit to their paths at the start. The pursuing player receives $1$ if capture
occurs within $H$ steps and $0$ otherwise; the evader receives the opposite
payoff. Capture includes occupying the same cell or exchanging positions
during a move.

**Possible experiment setup.**

- Begin with small maps, fixed initial positions, and vary the horizon.
  Enumerate all legal plans and solve the full matrix game by linear programming
  to check Double Oracle's value and full-game best-response gap.
- Repeat Double Oracle from several randomly chosen initial restricted strategy
  sets, recording the seeds. Compare total runtime, iterations, generated
  rows and columns, and payoff evaluations. Include the cost of computing
  best responses and constructing payoffs in the timings.
- Increase the horizon or map size and investigate when the full matrix becomes
  impractical and which part of Double Oracle dominates the computation.

In your proposal, specify both best-response oracles and a stopping tolerance.
Exhaustive search provides an initial oracle for small instances; justify the
accuracy of any faster replacement.

## Learning equilibrium strategies: fictitious play versus regret matching {#sec-project-learning-equilibria}

Investigate how players learn equilibrium strategies through repeated play.
Implement [fictitious play](../lectures/06-learning-in-games.qmd#sec-learning-fp)
and [external regret matching](../lectures/06-learning-in-games.qmd#sec-learning-regret-matching)
from Lecture 6. Focus on two-player zero-sum games, using the
[connection between regret and equilibrium](../lectures/06-learning-in-games.qmd#sec-learning-regret-zero-sum)
to evaluate the results.

**Possible application: learning to play Morra.**

Use [Morra from Lecture 4](../lectures/04-two-player-zero-sum-games.qmd#sec-zero-sum-morra),
where players simultaneously choose a number of fingers and guess the other
player's number.
Let both players learn from repeated interaction. How quickly do their empirical
strategy frequencies approach equilibrium, and how does this depend on the
learning rule and initialization? Compute an equilibrium by
[linear programming](../lectures/04-two-player-zero-sum-games.qmd#sec-zero-sum-lp)
as a benchmark.

**Possible experiment setup.**

- Validate the updates on the short matching-pennies examples in Lecture 6,
  then compare both methods in Morra over increasing numbers of rounds.
- Record the full-game saddle-point gap of the empirical strategy frequencies,
  each player's average external regret, and computation time. Plot current
  play separately from empirical frequencies to distinguish cycling from
  convergence of averages.
- Repeat stochastic runs with recorded seeds and vary initial play or
  fictitious-play tie-breaking. Report variation across runs and the number
  of rounds needed to reach a chosen accuracy.

In your proposal, specify the feedback available to each learner, update timing,
initialization, and evaluation metric. Choose a focused question about learning
speed or sensitivity to these choices, and interpret the findings using the
convergence results from the lecture.
